screens.title: Geospatial Queries and Text Search
screens.subtitle: Using GeoJSON, 2dsphere indexes, $near, $geoWithin, and text indexes for efficient location and full-text queries

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn two powerful features of MongoDB that solve different but related search problems. First, we’ll explore geospatial queries: how to store locations in GeoJSON, why a 2dsphere index is required, and how to ask questions like which places are nearest or which points lie inside a polygon or box. You’ll see concrete query forms for $near with $maxDistance and for $geoWithin with Polygon, Box, and center-sphere circle shapes. Second, we’ll cover basic text search: creating a text index across fields, how stemming and stop words affect results, and how to use $text with $search to retrieve and sort by relevance using $meta textScore. Throughout, I’ll point out common mistakes — like forgetting the 2dsphere index or creating multiple separate text indexes — and practical trade-offs when you might prefer regex, Atlas Search, or an external engine for advanced needs. By the end you’ll be able to index locations and text, run proximity and containment queries, and pick the right approach for common app scenarios.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Location and text search power many applications. Correct indexing and query patterns make these operations efficient and correct at scale.

narration.text: In the first set of objectives we focus on geospatial capability. You will learn to store location data in GeoJSON formats, first with Point and then with Polygon shapes for areas. You’ll create a 2dsphere index on the field that holds these GeoJSON objects so MongoDB can compute distances and containment on an earth-like sphere. Then you’ll run proximity searches using the $near operator and constrain results with $maxDistance, which is expressed in meters when used with 2dsphere. Each objective includes a small rationale: storing geometry with GeoJSON ensures standardized coordinates, indexing makes queries fast, and $near with $maxDistance is the typical pattern for "find nearby" features in apps. For each objective I’ll show code examples during the demo. A common pitfall you’ll avoid after this section is running spatial queries without a 2dsphere index, which causes slow execution or errors.

screens.title: GeoJSON Types: Point, Polygon, LineString
screens.subtitle: How MongoDB represents geographic features with standardized geometry objects

narration.text: GeoJSON is the format MongoDB uses to represent geographic data. The three most common types you'll use are Point, Polygon, and LineString. A Point encodes a single position as an array with longitude then latitude. A Polygon is an array of linear rings: the first ring defines the outer boundary and the first and last coordinate must be the same to close the shape. LineString represents a path through multiple coordinates. Using these standard types matters because MongoDB's geospatial operators and indexes expect GeoJSON objects to compute distances and containment correctly. For example, if you store a restaurant location as { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [ -73.9667, 40.78 ] } you can later run proximity queries against that field. A common misconception is thinking latitude comes first; GeoJSON uses longitude first. Another pitfall is forgetting to close polygon rings, which makes the geometry invalid. Takeaway: use GeoJSON to represent precise locations and areas, follow the coordinate order strictly, and validate geometry before indexing. How will you ensure your application always writes coordinates in longitude-latitude order? GeoJSON Types: Point, Polygon, LineString means point = [lon, lat]; polygon = rings with first and last identical; order matters for queries and indexes.. In practical terms, how mongodb represents geographic features with standardized geometry objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: GeoJSON basics
keyIdea.text: Point = [lon, lat]; Polygon = rings with first and last identical; order matters for queries and indexes.

content.html:
Definition
GeoJSON types
GeoJSON standardizes geographic features. Use Point for single coordinates and Polygon for areas. Coordinate order is longitude, latitude.
Examples
{
  "type": "Point",
  "coordinates": [ -74.0050, 40.7150 ]
}

{
  "type": "Polygon",
  "coordinates": [ [ [0,0],[3,6],[6,1],[0,0] ] ]
}
Why this matters
  • Operators like $near and $geoWithin expect valid GeoJSON to compute results correctly.
  • Wrong coordinate order produces incorrect results on the map and in distance calculations.
  • Invalid polygons will be rejected or give inaccurate containment checks.
Concrete analogy
Think of Point as a pushpin on a map and Polygon as a drawn fence. The fence's start and end must meet or it won't enclose space correctly.
Key Takeaway

GeoJSON is required format for spatial operators; always use [longitude, latitude] and validate polygons.

screens.title: Creating a 2dsphere Index
screens.subtitle: Prepare your collection for spherical geospatial queries

narration.text: A 2dsphere index is the cornerstone of efficient geospatial queries in MongoDB when working with GeoJSON. To create one, identify the field that holds your GeoJSON objects — commonly named location — and run createIndex with the value "2dsphere". This index tells MongoDB to interpret coordinates as points on a sphere, enabling distance calculations in meters and correct containment logic. For example, in the mongo shell you run db. restaurants. createIndex({ "location": "2dsphere" }). If you forget this step, operators like $near and $geoWithin will either fail or perform as collection scans. Another important detail is data consistency: ensure every document's location field is present and uses GeoJSON; mixed formats like legacy coordinate pairs can complicate indexing. After creating the index, you can verify it with getIndexes and watch query plans to see the index used. Misconception to clear up: 2dsphere is for GeoJSON spherical calculations, while the older 2d index targets planar coordinate data. Final takeaway: always create the 2dsphere index on your GeoJSON field before running spatial queries. Creating a 2dsphere Index means run createindex on your geojson field with type 2dsphere to enable correct spherical queries.. In practical terms, prepare your collection for spherical geospatial queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Index step
keyIdea.text: Run createIndex on your GeoJSON field with type 2dsphere to enable correct spherical queries.

content.html:
Steps
Create a 2dsphere index
  1. Confirm your field stores GeoJSON Points or Polygons.
  2. Run createIndex on that field with value "2dsphere".
  3. Verify with getIndexes and test with a small $near query.
Command (mongo shell)
db.restaurants.createIndex({ "location": "2dsphere" })

// Verify
db.restaurants.getIndexes()
Why this matters
Without the 2dsphere index, spatial operators cannot run efficiently. The index enables meter-based $maxDistance and proper spherical math used by $near.
Common mistake
Creating a non-GeoJSON field or creating a 2d index by mistake. Use 2dsphere for GeoJSON shapes intended for earth calculations.
Key Takeaway

Always create a 2dsphere index on your GeoJSON field before running $near or $geoWithin queries.

screens.title: $near and $maxDistance
screens.subtitle: Perform proximity searches and limit results by radius in meters

narration.text: Proximity search is one of the most common geospatial operations: find documents nearest a point and limit how far you look. MongoDB's $near operator takes a $geometry value — a GeoJSON Point — and optionally $maxDistance in meters when using a 2dsphere index. A typical query finds restaurants or events near a coordinate and returns them ordered by distance. In practice you write a find with location: { $near: { $geometry: { type: "Point", coordinates: [lon, lat] }, $maxDistance: 5000 } }. Remember $maxDistance is in meters for 2dsphere; if you omit it, results will include all distances but still be ordered by proximity. A common error is misplacing latitude and longitude or not having the 2dsphere index which prevents the operator from using optimized calculations. Concrete example: to find restaurants within 5 kilometers of [-73.9667, 40.78] you use $maxDistance: 5000. Takeaway: use $near for ranked, distance-ordered results and always confirm units and coordinate order before relying on distances in your UI. $near and $maxDistance means $near with $geometry and $maxdistance (meters) returns documents ordered by distance when a 2dsphere index exists.. In practical terms, perform proximity searches and limit results by radius in meters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Proximity query
keyIdea.text: $near with $geometry and $maxDistance (meters) returns documents ordered by distance when a 2dsphere index exists.

content.html:
Command demo
Find within 5 km
db.restaurants.find({
  "location": {
    "$near": {
      "$geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [ -73.9667, 40.78 ] },
      "$maxDistance": 5000
    }
  }
})
This returns documents ordered by proximity from the point specified. Ensure createIndex({ "location": "2dsphere" }) has been run.
Notes & units
When using 2dsphere, $maxDistance is in meters. If you need radians use $centerSphere with conversion.
Common mistake
Swapping latitude and longitude leads to incorrect regions. GeoJSON expects [longitude, latitude].
Key Takeaway

$near returns distance-ranked results; use $maxDistance in meters with a 2dsphere index to constrain radius.

screens.title: $geoWithin: Polygon Example
screens.subtitle: Select documents whose location is entirely contained within a polygon

narration.text: $geoWithin selects documents where the stored GeoJSON geometry lies entirely inside a supplied shape. A common use case is finding points inside a complex boundary such as a service area or neighborhood polygon. To use Polygon with $geometry you supply a valid GeoJSON Polygon with rings. Remember the outer ring must both start and end at the same coordinate. For example, a query might look like db. restaurants. find({ "location": { "$geoWithin": { "$geometry": { "type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [ [ [0,0], [3,6], [6,1], [0,0] ] ] } } } }). This returns only documents whose location point is inside that polygon. A misconception is thinking $geoWithin returns documents that intersect; it requires containment. If you need shapes that intersect rather than are contained, consider $geoIntersects. Concrete example: use $geoWithin for searching events happening inside an administrative boundary. Takeaway: validate polygon rings, ensure 2dsphere index exists, and choose the operator ($geoWithin vs $geoIntersects) that matches your inclusion intent. $geoWithin: Polygon Example means $geowithin with a polygon returns documents whose geometry is completely inside the specified geojson polygon.. In practical terms, select documents whose location is entirely contained within a polygon. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Containment query
keyIdea.text: $geoWithin with a Polygon returns documents whose geometry is completely inside the specified GeoJSON polygon.

content.html:
Example
Find points inside a polygon
db.restaurants.find({
  "location": {
    "$geoWithin": {
      "$geometry": {
        "type": "Polygon",
        "coordinates": [ [ [ 0, 0 ], [ 3, 6 ], [ 6, 1 ], [ 0, 0 ] ] ]
      }
    }
  }
})
Ensure the polygon's first and last point are identical to close the ring, otherwise the geometry is invalid.
Use case
Find all events entirely inside a festival boundary or a city's administrative polygon.
Misconception
$geoWithin requires containment; it does not return items that merely intersect the polygon edge. Choose $geoIntersects for intersection checks.
Key Takeaway

Use $geoWithin with valid closed polygons to select documents entirely inside an area.

screens.title: $geoWithin with Box and Circle
screens.subtitle: Quick patterns for rectangular and circular containment checks

narration.text: MongoDB offers compact forms for common shape queries. For rectangles you can use $box with two corner coordinates: the lower-left and upper-right. This is useful for axis-aligned bounding-box queries like a viewport selection. For circles, $centerSphere expresses a center point and radius in radians; convert meters by dividing by the earth radius in kilometers and converting units appropriately. Example: $geoWithin: { $box: [ [ -74, 40 ], [ -73, 41 ] ] } finds points in that rectangle. For circles use $centerSphere with radius in radians, for example [ [ -73.9667, 40.78 ], 5 / 6378.1 ] where 5 is kilometers and 6378.1 is the Earth's radius in kilometers. A common error is treating the radius for center-sphere as meters; it must be radians. Boxes are fast and convenient for rectangular filters but cannot represent rotated or irregular regions. Circles are natural for radius searches but remember conversion. Takeaway: pick $box for quick viewport filters and $centerSphere when you need true circular regions with spherical math. Always test results visually when possible. $geoWithin with Box and Circle means $box for rectangular bounds; $centersphere for spherical circles where radius is expressed in radians.. In practical terms, quick patterns for rectangular and circular containment checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Box vs Circle
keyIdea.text: $box for rectangular bounds; $centerSphere for spherical circles where radius is expressed in radians.

content.html:
Box example
db.restaurants.find({
  "location": { "$geoWithin": { "$box": [ [ -74, 40 ], [ -73, 41 ] ] } }
})
Use when you need all points inside an axis-aligned rectangle.
Circle example
db.restaurants.find({
  "location": {
    "$geoWithin": { "$centerSphere": [ [ -73.9667, 40.78 ], 5 / 6378.1 ] }
  }
})
Radius is in radians; convert kilometers by dividing by earth radius in kilometers.
When to use box
Viewport filters and rectangular regions aligned to latitude/longitude axes.
When to use circle
Radius-based searches like "within 10 km" where spherical math is required.
Key Takeaway

Choose the shape that matches your UI requirement and convert units correctly for spherical math.

screens.title: Text Indexes and $text Operator
screens.subtitle: Create a single text index and query with $text and $search

narration.text: Text indexes let MongoDB perform tokenized, stemmed full-text search across string fields. You create a single text index on one or more fields by specifying "text" as the index type, for example db. articles. createIndex({ "title": "text", "description": "text" }). When you index multiple fields you can assign weights so matches in higher-weighted fields rank higher in the relevance score. The $text operator with $search performs the query; wrap phrases in double quotes for exact phrase matching and prefix terms with a hyphen to exclude them. MongoDB tokenizes input, applies stemming, and removes stop words at index time, which makes searches efficient but also affects exact-match expectations. Use projection with { score: { $meta: "textScore" } } and sort by that meta value to return results ordered by relevance. A common misconception is that $text does substring matching like regex; it performs word-based matching and normalization. Takeaway: create a single combined text index, set weights for field importance, and use $meta textScore to surface the best matches. Text Indexes and $text Operator means a single text index tokenizes and stems text fields; query with $text and project $meta textscore for relevance.. In practical terms, create a single text index and query with $text and $search. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Text index basics
keyIdea.text: A single text index tokenizes and stems text fields; query with $text and project $meta textScore for relevance.

content.html:
Index example
db.articles.createIndex({ "title": "text", "description": "text" })

// With weights
db.articles.createIndex(
  { "title": "text", "description": "text" },
  { weights: { title: 5, description: 1 } }
)
Query example
db.articles.find(
  { "$text": { "$search": "MongoDB database" } },
  { "score": { "$meta": "textScore" } }
).sort({ "score": { "$meta": "textScore" } })
Key Takeaway

Text indexes provide efficient full-text search with stemming and stop-word removal. Use weights and textScore to tune relevance.

screens.title: Phrase Search and Exclusion with $text
screens.subtitle: Refine queries using quoted phrases and hyphen exclusions

narration.text: The $search string supports simple operators to refine text queries. Use double quotes to require an exact phrase and prefix terms with a hyphen to exclude them. For example, to find documents that contain the exact phrase data science but do not mention machine learning you write a search string like "\"data science\" -\"machine learning\"". Project the relevance score with { score: { $meta: "textScore" } } and then sort by that score to present the most relevant results first. Remember that stemming and stop words still apply: phrase queries are matched after tokenization and normalization, which can affect strict expectations. Also note that $text requires a text index to be present; otherwise the query will either error or not run. Concrete example: a find that returns score looks like db. documents. find({ "$text": { "$search": "\"data science\" -\"machine learning\"" } }, { score: { $meta: "textScore" } }). sort({ score: { $meta: "textScore" } }). Takeaway: phrase and exclusion operators let you fine-tune results, but understand how tokenization and stemming might change the match boundaries. Phrase Search and Exclusion with $text means use quotes for exact phrases and hyphens to exclude terms; always project and sort by textscore for relevance ordering.. In practical terms, refine queries using quoted phrases and hyphen exclusions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refined search
keyIdea.text: Use quotes for exact phrases and hyphens to exclude terms; always project and sort by textScore for relevance ordering.

content.html:
Query pattern
db.documents.find(
  { "$text": { "$search": "\"data science\" -\"machine learning\"" } },
  { "score": { "$meta": "textScore" } }
).sort({ "score": { "$meta": "textScore" } })
Phrase enclosed in quotes must match; prefix with hyphen to exclude documents with that phrase.
Practical tip
Use weights to boost matches in title fields so phrase matches there outrank body matches.
Common misconception
Text search is not substring search; it is word-based and normalized by stemming and stop-word removal.

screens.title: Hands-on: Indexes and Queries for Events
screens.subtitle: Apply 2dsphere and text index patterns to the events collection

narration.text: Let's walk through the hands-on activity using the events collection. First create a 2dsphere index on the location field so geospatial queries will be efficient. Then create a single text index on name and description, assigning higher weight to name so matches there score higher. Once indexes exist you can run a proximity query to find events within 10,000 meters of the New York City point and a text query to find events matching the keywords "music festival". Also combine tag filtering with a bounding-box geospatial filter for cases like outdoor events within a rectangle. I will demonstrate the exact commands you can run in the mongo shell and explain expected results. Remember: only one text index per collection; include all searchable fields when creating that index. When testing, inspect getIndexes to confirm creation and use explain to verify index usage. Final reflection: these commands are the same patterns you will reuse in production to power location-aware search features. Hands-on: Indexes and Queries for Events means create 2dsphere and text indexes, run proximity and text queries, and combine tag filters with bounding boxes.. In practical terms, apply 2dsphere and text index patterns to the events collection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hands-on flow
keyIdea.text: Create 2dsphere and text indexes, run proximity and text queries, and combine tag filters with bounding boxes.

content.html:
Starter commands
// 1. Create 2dsphere index
db.events.createIndex({ "location": "2dsphere" })

// 2. Create text index with weights
db.events.createIndex({ "name": "text", "description": "text" }, { weights: { name: 5, description: 1 } })
Sample queries
// 3. Events within 10km of NYC
db.events.find({
  "location": { "$near": { "$geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [ -74.0060, 40.7128 ] }, "$maxDistance": 10000 } }
})

// 4. Text search "music festival" sorted by relevance
db.events.find(
  { "$text": { "$search": "\"music festival\"" } },
  { "score": { "$meta": "textScore" } }
).sort({ "score": { "$meta": "textScore" } })

// 5. Tagged outdoor events within a box
db.events.find({
  "tags": "outdoor",
  "location": { "$geoWithin": { "$box": [ [ -74.02, 40.70 ], [ -73.98, 40.72 ] ] } }
})
Key Takeaway

Follow the createIndex patterns, verify with getIndexes, and combine text and geospatial filters to build location-aware search UX.

screens.title: Text Search vs Regex and Advanced Options
screens.subtitle: When to use $text, when to prefer $regex, and when to adopt richer search engines

narration.text: Choosing between $text and $regex depends on your goals. Use $text when you need full-text semantic search across fields with stemming, stop-word removal, and relevance scoring. $text is efficient because it relies on a text index, and it supports phrase and exclusion syntax. Use $regex when you need exact substring matches, case-sensitive patterns, or patterns that $text's tokenization would alter. Regex is powerful but can be slow on large collections without supporting indexes. For advanced scenarios such as fuzzy matching, synonyms, complex ranking, or language-aware tokenization beyond stemming, consider Atlas Search or external engines like Lucene-based systems. The practical workflow is to start with $text for general full-text needs, use $regex for narrow pattern matching, and migrate to richer tools when requirements grow. A misconception to clear up: $text is not a drop-in replacement for substring matching; think in terms of word tokens and relevance. Takeaway question: for your application, does relevance ranking or exact substring matching matter more? Text Search vs Regex and Advanced Options means $text is for relevance and tokenized search; $regex is for exact patterns. use richer engines for fuzzy or synonym-aware features.. In practical terms, when to use $text, when to prefer $regex, and when to adopt richer search engines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Search trade-offs
keyIdea.text: $text is for relevance and tokenized search; $regex is for exact patterns. Use richer engines for fuzzy or synonym-aware features.

content.html:
Use $text when
  • You want stemming and token-based matching.
  • Relevance ranking matters.
  • Searching across multiple fields together.
Use $regex when
  • You need exact substring or pattern matches.
  • Case-sensitive or anchored searches are required.
  • Dataset is small or properly indexed for regex patterns.
When to upgrade

For fuzzy matching, synonyms, or complex ranking consider Atlas Search or an external search engine built on Lucene.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Validation Steps
screens.subtitle: A short checklist to ensure correct geospatial and text search behavior

narration.text: Before you ship location or text search features, run a short checklist. First, ensure GeoJSON coordinate order is longitude then latitude everywhere you insert data. Second, verify that you created a 2dsphere index on the GeoJSON field and inspect getIndexes. Third, test $near and $geoWithin queries with known sample points to confirm distances and containment. Fourth, for text search create a single text index across your chosen fields and check that your weighting achieves the intended result by observing textScore. Fifth, remember a collection can only have one text index; include all searchable fields in it. Also test edge cases: empty or missing location fields, invalid polygons, stop words causing unexpected matches, and phrase searches that may tokenize differently. A common trap is relying on $text for substring needs — in that case evaluate $regex performance or a richer search solution. Final takeaway: validate data format, confirm indexes, run sample queries, and inspect results with explain to ensure index usage. keyIdea.title: Validation checklist
keyIdea.text: Confirm coordinate order, create and verify indexes, run sample queries, and inspect explain plans before production.

content.html:
Pre-release checklist
  1. Verify GeoJSON coordinate order is [longitude, latitude].
  2. Create and confirm a 2dsphere index on the location field.
  3. Run $near and $geoWithin test queries and validate results with known points.
  4. Create a single text index for all searchable fields and tune weights if needed.
  5. Use explain() to confirm queries use the intended index.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Core geospatial ideas to keep in mind

narration.text: Here are the core geospatial concepts you will refer to often. GeoJSON is the standard format MongoDB expects for geographic data; use Point for single coordinates and Polygon for areas, and always write coordinates as longitude then latitude. The 2dsphere index is required for correct spherical geometry calculations and efficient proximity or containment queries; without it $near and $geoWithin won’t perform well. The $near operator returns documents ordered by distance to a given GeoJSON point and accepts $maxDistance in meters when used with 2dsphere. These three building blocks — GeoJSON, 2dsphere, and $near with $maxDistance — form the foundation of location-aware features. Keep a short validation checklist to confirm coordinate order, index presence, and example query results before moving to production. Which of these concepts will you apply first in your project?

screens.subtitle: Core text search ideas and final reminders

narration.text: Here are core ideas for text search. A text index tokenizes, stems, and strips stop words to support efficient full-text search. You can create a single text index across multiple fields and assign weights to boost important fields such as title. Use the $text operator with $search to query that index, and project $meta textScore to retrieve relevance scores, then sort by that meta value to present results ranked by relevance. Remember a collection can only have one text index; plan fields and weights accordingly. Finally, be mindful of trade-offs: $text is great for relevance and multilingual stemming, $regex remains the tool for exact substring or anchored patterns, and for advanced fuzzy or synonym features consider richer search systems. Keep a short testing routine: verify index creation, run representative queries, and inspect explain plans to ensure the index is used.
